headline: Apple cannot make foldable iPhones fast enough

sources.title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out (BBC)
Apple's stock drops on weak margin forecast in Ternus' first earnings report (CNBC)
Apple FYQ4 Revenue Tops Forecasts On iPhone Sales As New CEO John Ternus Steps Up (Deadline)

chunks.text: Apple cannot make its new folding phone fast enough. Buyers {{snapped up}} the 1,999-dollar iPhone Duo, and it {{sold out}} soon after going on sale on October 23, 2026. Expected [[delivery dates]] for some orders were {{pushed back}} to 2027. On November 2, Apple's [[chief operating officer]], who runs its [[daily business]], said it is very hard to predict when [[supply]], the number of phones, will match [[demand]], the number people want.

verbs.wrong: To return something to a store
verbs.why: Shoppers snap up cheap tickets in minutes. Collectors snap up old toys at local fairs. Buyers snapped up the 1,999-dollar iPhone Duo.

verbs.correct: To have none left to sell
verbs.wrong: To show a product in a store
verbs.why: Popular concerts sell out in a few hours. Fresh bread sells out early at our bakery. The iPhone Duo sold out soon after it went on sale.

verbs.correct: To move something to a later time
verbs.wrong: To print a date on a receipt
verbs.why: Airlines push back flights when the weather is bad. Schools push back exams when teachers are sick. Expected delivery dates for some Duo orders were pushed back to 2027.

chunks.text: He spoke on an [[earnings call]], a meeting where a company explains its sales and profits to financial experts. It was the first for John Ternus, who replaced Tim Cook as Apple's [[chief executive]] on September 1. Apple {{took in}} 114.48 billion dollars in the three months ending September 26, up 12 percent from a year earlier. iPhones {{made up}} just over half of that money, and iPhone sales {{went up}} about 17 percent. Those numbers do not include the Duo.

verbs.correct: To earn an amount of money
verbs.wrong: To pay an amount of tax
verbs.why: Movie theaters take in the most money in summer. A busy restaurant takes in thousands of dollars a week. Apple took in 114.48 billion dollars in three months.

verbs.correct: To form part of a total
verbs.wrong: To grow faster than a total
verbs.why: Women make up half of our team. Students make up most of the town's population. Sales of iPhones made up just over half of Apple's money in those three months.
Rents go up every year in big cities. Food prices go up when gas costs more. Sales of iPhones went up about 17 percent.

chunks.text: Ternus faces a cost problem. Apple is paying much more for [[memory chips]], the parts that store photos and apps. Ternus called the increases [[unprecedented]], meaning never seen before. The [[boom]] in artificial intelligence has {{driven up}} prices, because [[data centers]], buildings full of computers, need so much memory. Apple has {{passed on}} part of the cost to buyers, raising iPhone prices by 100 dollars. A business news channel says many people are {{holding on to}} old computers for longer.

verbs.why: Bad weather drives up the price of fruit. High demand drives up the cost of plane tickets. The boom in artificial intelligence has driven up memory prices.

verbs.correct: To make someone else pay a cost
verbs.wrong: To write a cost in a report
verbs.why: Stores pass on higher costs to shoppers. Many landlords pass on new fees to their renters. Apple has passed on part of its memory costs to buyers.

verbs.correct: To keep something, not replace it
verbs.wrong: To fix something at a repair shop
verbs.why: Many families hold on to old cars for years. Some people hold on to phones until they stop working. A business news channel says many people are holding on to old computers for longer.

chunks.text: Apple's [[forecast]] for its [[profit margin]], the share of sales money left after costs, {{fell short of}} what experts expected. Its [[stock price]] dropped about 3 percent after the news. Some Duo buyers have seen their screens [[crack]] [[along the fold]]. Apple said in October a small number of phones were [[affected]], and promised to replace them. Executives did not {{bring up}} the issue on the call.

verbs.correct: To be lower than what was expected
verbs.wrong: To be the same as an earlier one
verbs.why: Many new movies fall short of what studios expect. Small shops often fall short of their sales goals. Apple's forecast fell short of what experts expected.
My boss brings up money at every meeting. Reporters bring up hard questions at press events. Apple's executives did not bring up the cracked screens on the call.

mainIdea.s: Apple's new chief executive gave his first report as buyers wanted more folding iPhones than the company could make. Sales rose, but memory costs and cracked screens are real problems.
mainIdea.why: Buyers snapped up the Duo, and Apple cannot say when supply will match demand. The boom in artificial intelligence has also driven up memory prices.

mainIdea.s: Apple's new leader reported strong sales and said supply of the Duo will match demand by December. Cheaper memory chips have made the phone easier to build and more profitable.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Apple cannot predict when supply will match demand, and expected delivery dates for some orders were pushed back to 2027. Memory chips also cost more now.

mainIdea.s: Apple has announced that it will stop selling iPads next year in order to build more laptops. Workers at several American factories will train for that change over the next two years.
mainIdea.why: Apple did not announce this. Its news on November 2 was its results, and sales of iPhones made up just over half of its money.

tf.s: Buyers snapped up the iPhone Duo, and it quickly sold out.
tf.why: The 1,999-dollar phone sold out soon after it went on sale, and expected delivery dates for some orders were pushed back to 2027.

tf.s: Apple knows exactly when there will be enough Duo phones for buyers.
tf.why: Its chief operating officer said this is very hard to predict. Expected delivery dates for some orders were already pushed back to 2027.

tf.s: The boom in artificial intelligence has driven up memory prices.
tf.why: Huge data centers need so much memory that prices have risen, and Apple is paying much more for memory chips.

tf.s: Apple passed on none of its higher memory costs to buyers.
tf.why: Apple has passed on part of the cost to buyers by raising iPhone prices.

tf.s: Apple's executives did not bring up the cracked screens on the call.
tf.why: Some Duo screens have cracked along the fold, but executives did not bring up the issue. Apple had already promised to replace those phones.

tf.s: Experts were pleased by Apple's forecast for its profit margin.
tf.why: The forecast fell short of what experts expected, and Apple's stock price dropped after the news.

lines.text: Did you try to get that folding iPhone?
No. Two thousand dollars for a phone? I don't have [[money to burn]].
Plenty of people do. Buyers {{snapped up}} the Duo, and it {{sold out}} fast.
So Apple can't make enough of them?
Right. Expected delivery dates for some orders were {{pushed back}} to 2027.
Well, that's [[a good problem to have]].
Maybe. An Apple executive says it's very hard to predict when supply will match demand.
How did the new CEO do on his first earnings call?
John Ternus sounded happy. Apple {{took in}} over 114 billion dollars in three months, and iPhones {{made up}} just over half of it.
I heard memory chips are a problem, though.
They are. Huge AI data centers have {{driven up}} memory prices, and Apple has {{passed on}} part of the cost.
Those new prices are [[out of my price range]].
You're not alone. A business news channel says many people are {{holding on to}} old computers for longer.
What about those Duo screens that crack?
That's [[a sore subject]]. Executives didn't {{bring up}} the issue on the call.
Were investors happy with the report?
Not completely. The profit margin forecast {{fell short of}} what experts expected, and the stock price dropped.
Sounds like a [[trial by fire]] for the new CEO.

expressions.def: A topic that makes someone upset or uncomfortable
